scenes.title: Foundation: functions of two variables

ask.q: For z=f(x,y), what does fₓ measure?
ask.nudge: Change x while holding y fixed.

body: A function of two variables assigns a scalar z=f(x,y) to each point (x,y). A partial derivative measures change in one coordinate while the other is held fixed.
The total derivative accounts for all ways the variables change along a path. It combines partial derivatives with the rates of change of the input variables.

items.ask: Define a partial derivative with respect to x.
refresh: Treat y as a constant and differentiate with respect to x. The definition is a one-variable difference quotient with the other coordinate frozen.
For f=x²y+3xy², fₓ=2xy+3y². The factor y is constant during the x differentiation, while y² is also constant.

items.recall: ∇f=(fₓ,fᵧ) for a scalar function of two variables.
refresh: The gradient collects all first partial derivatives into a vector. It points in the direction of steepest increase and its magnitude is the maximum directional derivative for a unit direction.
For f=x²+y², ∇f=(2x,2y). At (1,2), the gradient is (2,4).

items.ask: State the multivariable chain rule for z=f(x,y), x=x(t), y=y(t).
refresh: The output changes because both input coordinates may change. Multiply each partial derivative by the rate of its corresponding variable, then add the contributions.
This is the total derivative along a path. It differs from a partial derivative because neither input is necessarily held fixed.

scenes.title: Partial versus total change
scenes.objective: Distinguish a coordinate derivative from a path derivative.

ask.q: If x and y both depend on t, is dz/dt equal to fₓ alone?
ask.nudge: No, the y contribution must also be included.

body: A partial derivative asks what happens if one coordinate changes and the other is frozen. A total derivative asks what happens along an actual path where several coordinates may move.
The gradient is a vector of partial derivatives. Dotting it with a direction vector gives the directional derivative, which measures change in that direction.

scenes.title: First and second partial derivatives
scenes.objective: Compute repeated and mixed partial derivatives.

ask.nudge: Differentiate fₓ=2xy+3y² with respect to y.

blocks.body: fₓ=∂f/∂x with y fixed; fᵧ=∂f/∂y with x fixed.
If the relevant second partial derivatives are continuous in a neighbourhood, Clairaut's theorem gives fₓᵧ=fᵧₓ.

scenario.teaser: An outcome depends on two changing inputs.
scenario.title: Marginal effects in a two-input production function
body: A production function Q=f(K,L) depends on capital K and labour L. The partial derivative f_K measures the marginal product of capital while labour is held fixed.
The partial derivative f_L measures the marginal product of labour while capital is held fixed. If both inputs change over time, the total derivative combines both effects.
This distinction matters in comparative statics: a partial effect is not the same as the total observed change when multiple inputs move together.

scenes.title: Total differential and chain rule
scenes.objective: Compute change along a parameterised path.

ask.q: If z=f(x,y), x=x(t), y=y(t), write dz/dt.
ask.nudge: Use both partial derivatives and both input rates.

blocks.body: Each partial derivative is weighted by the rate at which its input changes. The total derivative is the sum of the two input contributions.

scenes.title: Guided: total derivative along a path
scenes.problem: Let z=x²+y², x=t and y=2t. Find dz/dt.
hints: Find the partial derivatives fₓ=2x and fᵧ=2y.

solution.say: dz/dt=2x(1)+2y(2). Substituting x=t and y=2t gives 2t+8t=10t.

scenes.title: Gradient and directional derivatives
scenes.objective: Find the rate of change in a specified direction.

ask.q: For f=x²+y² at (1,2), find the gradient.

blocks.body: ∇f=(fₓ,fᵧ). It points in the direction of steepest increase.
For a unit vector u=(u₁,u₂), Dᵤf=∇f·u=fₓu₁+fᵧu₂.
If the direction is given as a non-unit vector v, normalise it first: u=v/‖v‖. The directional derivative depends on direction, not the arbitrary length of v.

scenes.title: Guided: directional derivative
scenes.objective: Use the gradient and a unit direction.
scenes.problem: For f=x²+y² at (1,2), find the directional derivative in direction u=(3/5,4/5).
hints: Take the dot product with the given unit vector.

solution.say: The gradient is (2,4). Its dot product with (3/5,4/5) is 6/5+16/5=22/5.

ask.q: What is the maximum directional derivative at (1,2)?
ask.nudge: It is the magnitude of the gradient.

scenes.title: The gradient is steepest ascent

ask.q: For a differentiable scalar function, in which direction is the directional derivative largest?

body: The gradient points in the direction of the fastest local increase. Its magnitude is the maximum directional derivative over all unit directions.
A direction perpendicular to the gradient has zero first-order change. This is useful when interpreting contour maps: the gradient is normal to a level curve.

scenario.teaser: A response surface is explored by changing two inputs.
scenario.title: Steepest improvement on a response surface
body: Suppose a response z=f(x,y) represents yield, efficiency or a statistical objective. At a point, the gradient gives the direction of steepest local increase.
A unit direction u has directional derivative ∇f·u. Moving perpendicular to the gradient gives zero first-order change, which corresponds to moving along a level curve.
This local geometric interpretation supports optimisation algorithms and sensitivity analysis, but it does not by itself guarantee a global maximum.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.objective: Avoid common partial and total derivative errors.
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.claim: In fₓ, y is held fixed.
items.why: That is the definition of a partial derivative.

items.claim: The total derivative includes changes in both x and y.
items.why: It combines both partial derivatives with input rates.

items.claim: The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase.
items.why: Its dot product with a unit direction is maximised along the gradient.

items.claim: A directional derivative uses any vector without normalisation.
items.why: The standard directional derivative uses a unit direction vector.

items.claim: Continuous second partial derivatives imply fₓᵧ=fᵧₓ.
A partial derivative existing at a point always guarantees differentiability there.
items.why: Existence of partial derivatives alone is not sufficient.

scenes.title: Final multivariable-calculus checklist
scenes.objective: Choose the correct derivative for the question.
body: 1. Partial derivative: freeze the other variables.
2. Second partials: compute fₓₓ, fᵧᵧ and mixed terms carefully.
3. If second partials are continuous, mixed partials agree.
6. Gradient: ∇f=(fₓ,fᵧ); directional derivative: ∇f·u for unit u.
